title: A Consensus Glossary of Temporal Database Concepts
research_question: Can the temporal-database community establish precise, broadly accepted definitions and names for the core concepts needed to describe temporal data, histories, and multiple dimensions of time?
methodology: The paper reports a community consensus process rather than an empirical experiment. Candidate concepts were collected and revised through an open discussion process, including a June 1993 workshop involving 44 temporal-database researchers, followed by editorial revision. Concepts had to satisfy four relevance criteria, while names were assessed against nine naming criteria, and the resulting digest organizes the accepted concepts into general, temporal-database-specific, and specialized categories.

key_findings.finding: The glossary separates valid time, meaning when a fact is true in the modeled reality, from transaction time, meaning when that fact is current and retrievable in the database.
Transaction time is system-maintained, ordered consistently with database transactions, and does not permit rewriting past transaction-time values.

A bitemporal relation combines one system-supported valid-time dimension with one system-supported transaction-time dimension, providing distinct representations of real-world validity and database-record history.
The glossary defines history broadly enough to represent the temporal evolution of attributes, entities, relationships, schemas, transactions, and other database objects.
Snapshot equivalence provides a way to regard differently represented temporal relations as equivalent when they yield the same state at every instant.

The consensus process deliberately excluded concepts that were insufficiently defined, insufficiently understood, too general, or not widely used, favoring terminological stability over speculative terminology.

limitations: The paper is a terminology and consensus artifact rather than an empirical evaluation of temporal database implementations.
It is explicitly a digest of a larger glossary, so some naming discussions and supporting material are omitted from this version.
The consensus reflects the temporal-database community and state of research in the early 1990s rather than subsequent standards or implementation practice.
The definitions establish semantics but do not prescribe concrete provenance schemas, version-control mechanisms, or retrieval algorithms.
raw_claims: Valid time records when a database fact is true in the modeled world.
Transaction time records when a database fact is current and retrievable in the database.
Past transaction-time values are not intended to be altered.
A conventional relation with neither valid-time nor transaction-time timestamps is a snapshot relation.
A bitemporal relation carries both a valid-time dimension and a transaction-time dimension.
A history represents the temporal evolution of an object in the real world or database.
Histories can apply to attributes, entities, relationships, schemas, and transactions.
Snapshot equivalence compares temporal objects by their states at every instant.
The glossary only admits concepts judged temporal-specific, well-defined, well-understood, and widely used.
The consensus glossary was revised after discussion by a substantial group of temporal-database researchers.
